planting.note: Set out in spring in a mineral, fast-draining mix and disturb the taproot as little as possible; this dwarf species is one of the slowest-growing in the genus.

directions: Star cactus forms an almost flush-with-the-soil rosette of flattened, triangular tubercles arranged in a tight star pattern, each marked with a fine central groove of white felt rather than a true spine. It differs from its relatives A. fissuratus and A. retusus in its smaller size, smoother triangular tubercles, and much flatter, more geometric profile that barely rises above the surrounding gravel. Bright pink to magenta funnel-shaped flowers open from the woolly crown in autumn, often after the first cooling rains, and are large relative to the plant's tiny body. Grow in a shallow pot of gritty, mineral soil in full sun with minimal water outside the growing season, since the thick taproot rots quickly if kept damp while dormant.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Start seed indoors in a gritty mix or set out rooted offsets in spring; the heavy taproot needs a deep, well-drained container.

directions: Pygmy rebutia is a diminutive, extremely variable clustering species from the high Andes of Bolivia and Argentina, its short, nearly ground-hugging olive-green to purple-tinted stems barely rising above soil level and anchored by a taproot that can outweigh the visible plant. Unlike the more upright, cylindrical R. muscula or R. minuscula, this species stays flatter and more spherical, with faint spiraling ribs and short, fine bristly spines rather than showy centrals. Funnel-shaped flowers in shades from pale pink to orange-red appear at the base of the stem in late spring, often nearly hiding the plant body. Because it grows at high elevation it tolerates cooler nights and brighter light than many soft-bodied cacti, but demands sharp drainage and a dry winter rest to avoid rot.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Sow indoors on a mineral seed mix or set out established plants in spring; a coastal-climate species that appreciates bright light without extreme heat.

directions: Chilean ball cactus is a solitary to sparingly branched, globe-shaped to short-columnar species from the coastal cliffs and terraces of central Chile, where it clings to rock outcrops within reach of sea fog. Its bumpy, obtuse ribs are often almost hidden beneath dense, variably colored spination ranging from straw-yellow to blackish brown, giving established plants a shaggy, well-armored look distinct from the smoother-ribbed Gymnocalycium species it superficially resembles. Funnel-shaped flowers in cream, pink, or magenta open near the woolly crown in summer, followed by fleshy fruit. Despite its fog-desert origin it is an easy, xerophytic grower in cultivation, needing full sun, sharp drainage, and caution against overwatering in humid or poorly ventilated conditions.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Start indoors in a mineral mix or set out rooted plants in spring; give this coastal-desert species maximum sun and infrequent, careful watering.

directions: Islaya cactus is a solitary, globose-to-cylindrical species native to the fog-desert coast where northern Chile meets southern Peru, one of the most arid habitats on earth, where its only reliable moisture is the garua sea fog that condenses on its body overnight. Extremely woolly areoles and dense, dark, outward-spreading spines armor the stem against intense coastal sun and wind, a heavier and more rigid spination than is seen on the related Eriosyce subgibbosa. Funnel-shaped yellow flowers emerge from the woolly, felted crown in summer, followed by club-shaped pink to red fruit. In cultivation it demands a mineral, fast-draining substrate, bright light, and a light misting or drought-style watering regime that mimics its native fog rather than regular rainfall.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Start indoors in a mineral mix or set out established plants in spring; extremely slow-growing and best suited to container culture in most gardens.

directions: Long-stamened copiapoa is a slow, heavily clustering species from the Atacama coast of Chile that eventually forms large, dense mounds of 15 or more grey, wax-coated heads, each with orange wool filling the crown. It is closely allied to Copiapoa cinerea, sharing the same chalky epidermis meant to reflect the intense desert sun, but distinguishes itself by its more pear-shaped individual stems and denser, more tightly packed clustering habit as the mound ages; the waxy bloom often fades in cultivation, revealing green or brownish skin beneath. Yellow flowers open near the woolly apex in the warmer months, a modest display compared to the plant's striking sculptural form. Give it full sun, minimal water, and years of patience, since even container-grown specimens add only a little each season.

planting.note: Start indoors on a mineral seed mix or set out rooted plants in spring; an easy, adaptable species that tolerates a wider soil range than many chin cacti.

directions: Anisits' chin cactus is a light green, often reddish-tinged globular species from the lowland scrub of Bolivia and Paraguay, larger and more freely clustering with age than the smaller G. bruchii or G. andreae. Its eight to eleven ribs carry pointed humps and slender, twisted, yellowish-to-brown spines that curve close to the body, usually without a central spine, giving it a softer-looking armament than the stouter-spined G. saglionis. Large white-to-pink funnel-shaped flowers, sometimes several inches across, open from the crown in late spring and summer, followed by elongated red fruit. It is a notably polymorphic, easy-growing species that tolerates a touch more shade and humidity than most Gymnocalycium, making it a forgiving choice for beginners.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Start indoors in a gritty mix or set out rooted cuttings in spring; the sprawling stems root readily and look best in a hanging pot or raised bed edge.

directions: Thumb cactus is a slender, sprawling to creeping Mexican species named for botanist Eizi Matuda, its narrow cylindrical stems clustering from the base and trailing or arching rather than standing upright like M. elongata or M. gracilis. Fine, translucent white radial spines cover the stem almost like a soft fuzz, punctuated by a single pinkish-white central spine per areole that ages to dull white, and the bare, hairless axils separate it from woollier relatives such as M. bombycina. Small pale reddish-purple flowers ring the stem tips in spring, followed by slim green-and-red fruit. Its lax, cascading habit makes it a natural choice for hanging baskets or the edge of a raised bed, where it needs full sun, sharp drainage, and only occasional water to keep the thin stems from stretching or rotting.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online
Cactus and Succulent Society of America
